0.title: Fruitful to the End
0.essay:
Our culture prizes youth. Advertising, entertainment and even churches often focus on the young. Older people can feel invisible, unwanted or a burden. Scripture sees old age very differently.

Fears of ageing

Many people fear growing old: the loss of health, independence, friends, purpose and memory. Retirement, which promises leisure, can bring emptiness instead.

God’s view

“Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life” (Proverbs 16:31). “They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green” (Psalm 92:14). And God promises to carry his people all the way: “even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you” (Isaiah 46:4).

For whom

This study is for those who are growing older, and for those who love and care for them. It looks honestly at the losses of ageing, and hopefully at the fruitfulness God offers in the later years, the calling to pass on the faith, and the grace to finish well.

The chapters

The Crown of Gray Hair; The Losses of Age; Purpose in the Later Years; Passing On the Faith; and Dependence and Finishing Well.

For reflection

What do you most hope for, and most fear, about growing older?

1.title: The Crown of Gray Hair
1.essay:
In a world that hides wrinkles and celebrates youth, Scripture calls grey hair a crown. A long life of faithfulness is a glory, not something to be ashamed of.

Honour the aged

“You shall stand up before the gray head and honor the face of an old man, and you shall fear your God: I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:32). In Israel, respect for the elderly was tied to the fear of God. The old were to be honoured, consulted and cared for. That is not merely good manners. How we treat the old reflects how we view God.

A crown of glory

“Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life” (Proverbs 16:31). Age is not a loss to hide but a crown to wear. And each stage of life has its own beauty: “The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair” (Proverbs 20:29).

Wisdom

“Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days” (Job 12:12). Not every older person is wise. But those who have walked with God for many years have a wisdom the young need.

When Rehoboam became king, he rejected the counsel of the old men who had served his father Solomon, and “took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him” (1 Kings 12:8). His foolish decision split the kingdom. Despising the wisdom of the old has consequences.

God carries his people

“Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb; even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save” (Isaiah 46:3–4).

In the surrounding verses, Isaiah mocks idols that have to be carried by their worshippers. The living God is the opposite: he carries his people. The God who carried us as infants will carry us in old age. He does not abandon his people when they become weak.

Fruitful in old age

“The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God. They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green” (Psalm 92:12–14). And their lives have a purpose: “to declare that the LORD is upright; he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him” (Psalm 92:15).

Spiritual fruitfulness does not depend on physical strength. A long life can itself be a testimony to God’s faithfulness.

Against ageism

A culture that values people for their productivity or appearance will inevitably devalue the old. Scripture values people because they bear God’s image, at every age. And long life is often presented as a blessing: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land” (Exodus 20:12). Each additional year is a gift of grace.

Old and young together

In a healthy church, the old and the young need each other. The old bring wisdom and stability. The young bring energy and fresh vision. Neither is complete without the other.

Think of a church that deliberately includes its older members: asking them to share testimonies, mentor younger believers, and pray for the church. Younger members find their faith strengthened. Older members feel valued rather than sidelined.

For reflection

What wisdom have you received from older believers? How does your church honour its older members, and how could it do better?

2.title: The Losses of Age
2.essay:
Ageing brings real losses, and Scripture does not hide them. But it also shows how faith can deepen even as the body declines.

The body declines

Ecclesiastes 12 describes old age in vivid poetry. “Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, ‘I have no pleasure in them’” (Ecclesiastes 12:1). It speaks of the keepers of the house trembling, the grinders ceasing and the windows growing dim — images often taken as the hands, the teeth and the eyes — and of the fear of heights. Finally, “the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

Knowing one’s limits

Barzillai had supported King David during his exile. When David invited him to live at court, the old man declined: “I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women?” (2 Samuel 19:35). He asked David to honour his son instead. Barzillai faced his age with honesty and grace.

Fear of abandonment

“Do not cast me off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength is spent” (Psalm 71:9). Many older people fear being forgotten, by family, by society, even by God. The psalmist felt enemies taking advantage of his weakness. Yet he resolved, “But I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more” (Psalm 71:14). Old age did not end his praise. It deepened it.

Loss of loved ones

The longer we live, the more people we lose: spouses, friends, brothers and sisters, sometimes children. Grief becomes a frequent companion, and loneliness can be one of the hardest burdens of old age.

Think of a widow in her eighties who has outlived most of her friends. Her church arranges regular visits, and a young family adopts her as an honorary grandmother. She begins praying for them every day. Her loneliness eases, and her prayers become a gift to them.

Loss of memory

Some face dementia, which can take away memory and even personality. It is a hard road, for the person and for their family. Yet salvation does not depend on our remembering God, but on God remembering us. “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). He does not forget those who can no longer remember him. He knows and holds them still.

Lament is allowed

The losses of age are real, and believers may grieve them honestly before God, as the psalmists did. Pretending everything is fine is not faith. Bringing the losses to God is.

Inward renewal

“So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). The body declines, but the soul can grow. Many believers grow most in faith, patience and love in their last years. Paul goes on: present afflictions are “light momentary affliction” compared with “an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17).

Resurrection hope

The decline of the body is not the end. “What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power” (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). The aching joints, failing eyes and weakening heart are not the final word. A new body is coming.

For reflection

Which losses of ageing do you fear most? Is there an older person you know who is lonely, and how could you visit or include them this month?

3.title: Purpose in the Later Years
3.essay:
Our culture often presents retirement as one long holiday. There is nothing wrong with rest and enjoyment after years of work. But Scripture knows no retirement from serving God.

Caleb

Forty-five years after God’s promise to him, Caleb came to Joshua at eighty-five and said, “I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming. So now give me this hill country” (Joshua 14:11–12). It was the land where giants lived. He trusted God to help him take it. Few will have Caleb’s strength, but all can have his spirit.

Moses

“Now Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh” (Exodus 7:7). Moses’ most important work began at an age when most people would have stopped.

Simeon and Anna

When the infant Jesus was brought to the temple, two elderly believers recognised him. Simeon, who had been promised he would see the Messiah, took the baby in his arms and said, “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30).

Anna, a widow of great age, “did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day” (Luke 2:37). She spoke of the child “to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem” (Luke 2:38). God gave these two old people the privilege of being among the first to welcome his Son.

Older men and women

Paul gave specific instructions for older believers. “Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness” (Titus 2:2). Older women “are to teach what is good, and so train the young women” (Titus 2:3–4). Older believers are not on the sidelines. They have a ministry of example and teaching.

Ministries of the later years

Older believers can pray, perhaps the greatest ministry of all. They can mentor younger Christians, show hospitality, visit the sick, serve in church, volunteer in the community and share the gospel. Time, experience and wisdom are gifts to be used.

Some of the church’s greatest work is done by elderly saints on their knees. “The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working” (James 5:16). An older believer who can do little else can still pray, and those prayers matter.

Calling continues

A person’s calling is not only their paid work. Every believer is called to serve God and others throughout life. Retirement changes the shape of that calling, not its existence. Rest in later years is a gift. But a life of nothing but leisure rarely satisfies. Purpose and service bring joy at every age.

Think of a retired engineer who decides to use his skills and time for his church: helping with maintenance, mentoring young men, leading a weekly prayer meeting, and volunteering at a local charity. He says these are the most rewarding years of his life.

Stewarding resources

Many older people have savings and possessions. Scripture calls for generosity and wise planning, including making a will, supporting the work of the gospel, and providing for family. “A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children” (Proverbs 13:22).

Still full of sap

“They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green” (Psalm 92:14). The later years are a season to bear fruit, not to fade away.

For reflection

If you are retired or nearing retirement, how will you use these years for God? What could you learn from Caleb, Simeon and Anna?

4.title: Passing On the Faith
4.essay:
One of the great callings of old age is to pass on faith in God to the young.

Until I proclaim

“So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation, your power to all those to come” (Psalm 71:18). The psalmist had known God since his youth, and he saw his old age as having a purpose: to tell the next generation.

We will not hide them

Psalm 78 describes the task: “We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done” (Psalm 78:4). The goal: “so that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God” (Psalm 78:7). Faith passes from generation to generation through faithful telling.

Everyday conversation

Moses commanded God’s people to teach his words to their children, and to “talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Faith is passed on not only through formal teaching, but through everyday conversation, woven into ordinary life across the generations.

Grandparents

Paul reminded Timothy of “your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well” (2 Timothy 1:5). A grandmother’s faith shaped a future church leader. Grandparents have a unique opportunity to pray for, teach and encourage their grandchildren, and sometimes to be a steady spiritual presence when parents are not.

Telling your story

Older believers have stories of God’s faithfulness: answered prayers, hard seasons survived, lessons learned the hard way. These stories are precious to the young. Writing them down, or telling them aloud, is a gift.

Think of a grandfather who begins writing letters to each of his grandchildren, telling them how he came to faith, how God helped him through hard times, and what he prays for them. Years after his death, one grandson reads the letters and is moved to return to Christ.

Mentoring

Older Christians can mentor younger ones in faith, marriage, parenting, work and suffering. Younger believers often long for this, but do not know how to ask. Sometimes the older person needs to make the first move.

Praying for the young

Older believers who can do little else can pray faithfully for children, grandchildren and the young people of the church. These prayers may bear fruit long after they have died.

Across the generations

God’s promises extend across generations. “For the promise is for you and for your children” (Acts 2:39). He is the God “who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations” (Deuteronomy 7:9). Faith is not inherited automatically, and every person must come to Christ personally. But God often works through families.

When children have strayed

Many older believers grieve children or grandchildren who have left the faith. They can keep praying, keep loving, and trust God, who is able to save. The prodigal son came home.

The best legacy

The greatest legacy is not money or possessions, but faith passed on. A good inheritance for one’s children’s children (Proverbs 13:22) includes, above all, the knowledge of God.

For reflection

Who passed on the faith to you, and how? What story of God’s faithfulness could you tell a younger believer this month?

5.title: Dependence and Finishing Well
5.essay:
Many older people must learn to depend on others for things they once did themselves. That can be humbling and hard. But it can also teach grace, gratitude and trust.

Another will dress you

After his resurrection, Jesus told Peter, “when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go” (John 21:18). John explains that this pointed to the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. Then Jesus said to him, “Follow me” (John 21:19). Even dependence and death can be ways of following Christ.

Dependence and dignity

Needing help does not diminish a person’s dignity. Christ himself was carried as a baby, and another man helped him carry his cross. Dependence is part of being human. Learning to receive help graciously is part of growing in grace.

Caring for the elderly

Scripture commands families to care for their older members. “But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God” (1 Timothy 5:4). Paul’s words are strong: “if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). And the church has a responsibility to care for those who have no family: “to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27).

Hard decisions

Sometimes a family cannot provide the care an elderly relative needs, and a care home is the most loving option. That is not abandonment, if the family continues to visit, love and speak up for them. These decisions are painful, and families need the church’s support and prayer as they make them.

Numbering our days

“The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away” (Psalm 90:10). The right response is a prayer: “So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). Awareness of mortality leads to wisdom. Older believers can prepare for death practically and spiritually, putting their affairs in order and their hearts at peace. The Death, Dying and Heaven study explores this further.

Finishing well

Near the end of his life, Paul wrote, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Timothy 4:7–8). Finishing well means persevering in faith to the end, not drifting or becoming bitter.

Many in Scripture started well and finished badly. Solomon began with wisdom, but “when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4). His old age was a sad decline. Paul, by contrast, finished faithfully. Starting well is not enough. We need grace to finish well.

Bitter or gentle

Some people grow bitter, critical and fearful as they age. Others grow gentler, more grateful and more trusting. The difference is often the habits of a lifetime, and the grace of God. The kind of old person we become is being shaped now.

Think of a woman in her nineties who now lives in a care home and needs help with everything. She can no longer read her Bible, but she knows many psalms by heart. She recites them to the carers and thanks them for every kindness. They say she is the most grateful person they have ever looked after.

The best is ahead

Old age is preparation for glory. For the believer, the best days are not behind but ahead.

For reflection

What habits are you building now that will shape the kind of old person you become? How could you help an older believer finish well?
